192.    DR. M.N. DAS: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the country's outstanding external debt has shot up from 
$98.76 billion in March 2002 to US$ 104.99 billion in December, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether this will have a serious impact on the Indian economy; 
(c) whether the Government are confident that the country's foreign debt 
position is comfortable and economy is well insulated from possible external 
sector shocks; 
(d) if so, whether the latest status report of the Ministry of Finance has 
pointed out India's position as alarming; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
66 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(e) if so, what steps Government proposed to take to meet the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) The external debt stock of the 
country stood at 105.0 billion as at end-December, 2002 against 98.76 billion 
at end-March, 2002. Since important external debt indicators like debt-GDP 
ratio, debt service to current receipts ra tio and short term to total debts ratio 
have progressively shown improvement, a marginal increase in external debt 
is not expected to have any adverse impact on the Indian economy. 
(c) As the external debt indicators have improved substantially over time, 
external debt position of the country is comfortable. 
(d) and (e) No. Sir. The latest Status Report on India's External Debt 
points out that the incidence of external debt burden measured by the debt-GDP 
ratio has declined from 38.7 per cent at end-March, 1992 to 20.6 per cent at 
end-December, 2002, while debts service as per cent to Current Receipts 
declined from 30.2 per cent to 13.7 per cent in the corresponding period. 
Further, the short-term debt as a proporation to foreign exchange assets has 
declined from a high of 382.1 per cent to 5.0 per cent during the same period. 
Cautious and prudent approach towards external debt management pursued 
in 1990 by the Government of India ha s helped to place India in comfortable 
external debt position. The policy focus has been to concentrate on 
concessional and less expensive fund sources, preference for longer maturity 
profile, and enduring vigil on build up of short-term debt, premature 
retirement of high cost external debt and encouragement to non-debt creating 
capital flows.

208. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Will the Minister of FINANCE

ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) CRISIL have estimated that 
the gross NPAs of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) as on 31st March,

made by the rating agencies to not reflect the factual position, as these 
agencies have done the estimation of NPAs on the basis of a sample and extra 
polating the results to the entire system. CRISIL has applied a multiple to the 
reported gross NPAs in the Priority Sector "based on its understanding of the 
portfolio's profile" to arrive at the estimate of gross NPAs in the Priority 
Sector. For non Priority Sector's loans CRISIL has classified

resultant rating distribution and their default probability statistics to estimate

performing and added these to the reported NPAs.

Requirement vis-a-vis availability of water 
260. SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that accord ing to the WHO and UNICEF study 
water supply and sanitation in India would outstrip by 31 per cent by the 
middle of the century; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that according to that study, per capita annual 
requirement of water would be 1422 billion cubic metres and availability of 
water would be only 1086 billion cubic metres; and

matching the availability and utilisation of water for human consumption? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The 
report of the Planning Commission entitled "India Assessment 2002— Water 
Supply & Sanitation" (A WHO-UNICEF sponsored Study), indicates that 
country's total water requirement by the year 2050 will become 1422 Billion Cubic 
Metre (BCM), which will be much in excess of the total utilisable average water 
resources of 1085 BCM.Thus, as per the report, the estimated requirement of 2050 
will exceed utilisable water resources by 31%. 
(c) As per the assessment made by Central Water Commission, the total 
utilisable water resources of the country are 1122 BCM and 
118 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
the water requirements by the y ear 2050 are 1447 BCM. Besides full 
development of the utilisable water resources of 1122 BCM, another 200 
BCM of water is proposed to be utilized through inter-linking of rivers. For 
this purpose, National Water Development Agency has formulated National 
Perspective Plan for water resources development which envisages 
interlinking between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for 
transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit basins. In addition to this, it 
is planned to implement better management practices including re-cycling and 
re-use of water to bridge the gap between the availability and requirement.

†*13.   SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minsiter of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that import of a number of Indian goods is still 
restricted in various manners in several member countries of the World Trade 
Organisation; 
(b) if so, the names of such countries togetherwith the Indian goods 
restricted for import in these countries; and 
(c) the value of the exports made from  India to each of these countries 
during the years 2000-01, 2001-02 and 2002-03? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN* 
JAITLEY): (a) One of the fundamental principles of the multilateral trading system 
under WTO is that of the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) Treatment which 
envisages non-discrimination among member countries for the purpose of 
trade.Therefore, discrimination or restrictions specific to India goods by other 
WTO members is not permitted. However, WTO rules authorize restrictions 
on import of goods based on tariff as agreed upon and also through other types 
of restrictions which are permissible. Such permissible restrictions include 
those based on balance of payment grounds, sanitary and phyto sanitary related 
restrictions, conformity with 
†Origihal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
152 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
agreed/international standards and contingent protection measures like anti-
dumping, subsidy and safeguard actions. Procedural requirements could also 
act as barriers to trade. 
Restrictions on import of goods from India exist in several of the WTO 
member countries. When market access is affected in any significant manner 
in specific countries, such issues are taken up, particularly if they are also not 
WTO compatible. Normally such rest rictions on imports are addressed 
through bilateral contacts like inter-governmental commissions, working 
groups on trade and economic cooperation etc. The WTO also provides for a 
number of mechanisms for addressing the issue of restriction on imports of 
goods into the markets by WTO me mbers. These include Trade Policy 
Review Mechanism, discussions in the Councils, subsidiary bodies, bilateral 
consultations and dispute settlement. Such issues are also taken up as part of 
multilateral negotiations. 
(b) and (c) It would be difficult to list all the restrictions on imports from 
India in various WTO member countries or to name all of these countries 
since restrictions of one kind of or another exist in various Members. 
Department of Commerce has been compiling non-tariff barriers being faced 
by India in foreign markets from time to time.

modalities by Members to the Negotiating Group on Market Access for non-
agricultural goods. However, it was not included in the Annex listing the formula 
reduction methods submitted by Members. 
India refined its specific proposal by presenting it in a mathematical form 
with quantification of the flexibilities sought and submitted the same to the 
WTO on 14 March 2003 vide Document No. TN/MA/W/10 Add. 2. This 
revised submission was subsequently included in the Annex listing the formula 
methodologies in the revision of the WTO Secretariat's compilation presented 
to Members on 1 April 2003 vide Document No. TN/MA/6 Rev. 1 
It may also be mentioned that on 16 May 2003 the Chairman of the 
Negotiating Group on Market Access submitted on his own responsibility a set 
of draft modalities for Members consid eration. These.drafts, circulated vide 
Doucment No.TN/MAAA//35 is presently being discussed. 
158 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
India's tariff reduction proposal inter-alia required a simple percentage cut on 
bound tariffs of each Member, with a higher percentage to be set for developed 
countries than the percentage set for developing countries. Additionally, Members 
were required not to impose tariff on any product in excess of three times their 
average tariff. The average for this purpose was to be calculated after effecting 
the tariff reduction. 
While India did not specify what the reduction percentage would be for 
developed and developi ng countries, as an illu stration the reduction on 
different tariff lines using a 50-33.33% and 45-30% ratio was included in the 
paper. 
For unbound tariff lines, it was proposed that developing countries could 
bind them at the highest of the bound rates in a Member's tariff schedule or at 
the applied rate on a cut off date whichever was higher. 
Integral to the Indian proposal were also two provisions as special and 
differential measures for developing coun tries. These were (a) flexibility to 
decide individual tariff bindings on at least 15% of the bound tariff lines, on 
the understanding that the overall percentage reduction will be achieved; and 
(b) at least up to 10% of the presently unbound tariff lines considered sensitive 
or strategically important for a developing country could continue to be left 
unbound.

Agriculture sector provides livelihood for the large majority of the 
people in India and negotiations in agriculture should result in tangible 
improvement in the living conditions of low-income and resource poor 
farmers and landless agricultural labourers. This cannot be achieved unless 
there is significant and meaningful reduction in domestic support and all forms 
of export subsidies in major developed countries. Further more, concerns 
relating to food security and livelihood of farmers should be addressed through

apply safeguards to address different situations.

Known as DOTS, which is a WHO recommended strategy, is being

Ban on private blood banks 
72. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: W ill the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to ban private blood bank 
throughout the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the date from which the proposed ban is likely to be made effective? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) No Sir. The position is that 
the National Blood Policy, 2002 stipulates that "fresh licenses to stand-alone 
blood banks in the private sector shall not be granted. Renewal of such blood 
banks shall be subjected to thorough scrutiny and shall not be renewed in case 
of non-compliance of any condition of license". 
In pursuance of this stipulation, we would need to amend the relevant 
provisions in the Drugs and Cosmetic Rules, after which fresh licenses would 
not be granted to stand-alone blood banks in the private sector. 
This stipulation does not apply to the existing blood banks holding valid 
licenses and complying with the conditions of license. 
Management of medical waste 
73. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether recently a Parliamentary Committee has pointed out, in its 
report, instances of serious lapses on the part of the Government Hospitals 
and private nursing homes in the matter of management of biomedical 
wastes; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to give effect to the 
recommendations of the Committee? 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) The 112th Report of the 
Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment and Forests on Demands for Grants (2003-04) of 
the Ministry of Environment & Forests has, inter-alia observed that the 
scientific management of medical wastes is dangerously neglected in the 
country. The staff charged with the responsibility for sanitation, cleanliness in 
hospitals and other medical units seem to be ignorant of the regulation for 
bio-medical wastes disposal. The Committee recommended that persons in 
charge in small and big nursing homes and hospitals need to be trained 
regarding these aspects. 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests has informed that Central 
Pollution Control Board and State Pollution Control Boards conduct training 
courses and workshops for personnel of Healthcare Establishments and other 
concerned Departments. Central Pollution Control Board has also conducted 
two workshops at Hyderabad in assoication with Andhra Pradesh State 
Pollution Control Board and also one each at Delhi and Lucknow. The Central 
Pollution Control Board also has funded the State Pollution Control Boards of 
Gujarat, Jammu & Kashmir, Tamil Nadu, Assam, Himachal Pradesh and 
Chhattisgarh along with the required technical support to conduct workships 
on hospitals wastes management. The Ministry of Environment & Forests/ 
Central Pollution Control Board also supports training and awareness 
programmes conducted by NGOs, State Pollution Control Boards and other 
organisation with regard to the implementation of Bio-Medical Wastes 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 1998.

Long term action plan for development of film industry 
79. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any long term action plan for all round 
development of the film industry in the country; 
242 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether some States apart from de veloping infrastructure are also 
giving various incentives to the film industry; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) and (b) 
According to the Constitution of India 'Cinema' is a State subject, except 
'certification of films' which is on the Union List. However, the Central 
Government has taken several supportive measures for the overall 
development of the film industry. Some of these measures are given below:— 
• In order to facilitate a greater flow of institutional finance to the film 
industry, a Notification dated 16.10.2000 was issued by the Ministry 
of Finance whereunder 'entertainment industry, including films' has been 
specified as an approved activity for extending loans under the 
Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) Act. The Reserve Bank of 
India has also evolved guidelines to enable commercial banks to fund 
film production. 
• The Foreign Direct Investment re gime for films has been further 
liberalized in order to facilitate access to additional capital by the film 
industry. 
• A plan scheme has been included in the 10th Five Year Plan, to 
participate in film markets in I ndia and abroad with a view to 
providing exposure to Indian films in the global market. 
• Several steps have been taken to mitigate the menace of audio and 
video piracy like a recommendation by the Committee for 
development of the entertainment sector set up to suggest the policy 
framework both at the Centre and in the States, to fix a ceiling for 
entertainment tax at 60%, organization of training courses and 
removal of excise duty on CDs. 
• Good cinema is encouraged through the medium of National Film 
Awards. 
• In 2002 alongwith the International Film Festival of India, a Film 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
Bazaar has been initiated by the Government to provide a platform for 
interaction between Indian Film Industry and international buyers and 
sellers. 
• In the Budget of 2002-03 a five-year tax break has been given to 
multiplexes set up outside Municipal limits. 
• The best cinema in any year is selected as part of the 'Indian 
Panorama'. These films are especially shown to audiences on the 
festival circuit in order to create, as well as cater to, a taste for Indian 
cinema. 
• Students are trained to be film professionals in the Film and 
Television Institutes, Kolkata and Pune. 
• The National Film Development Corporation and the Children's Film 
Society of India finance production of film especially by new film 
makers. 
• Three International Film Festivals are organized by the Government 
of India to promote cinema. 
(c) and (d) Since 'cinema' is a State subject, detailed information in this 
regard is not maintained Centrally. However, it is understood that various 
State Governments offer incentives to their local film industry in the nature of 
subsidies, loans of entertainment tax exemptions.

Electronic Media TV;

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI S HANKAR PRASAD): (a) Detailed 
guidelines for starting DTH service we re issued in March, 2001. The 
guidelines, inter alia, provide that:— 
• The licensee company shall be an Indian company, registered under 
the Indian Companies Act, 1956; 
• Licensee shall adhere to programme and advertisement codes 
256 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
laid down by Ministry of Information and Broadcasting from time to 
time; 
• All foreign personnel likely to be deployed by way of appointment, 
contract, consultancy etc. by the licensee for installation, maintenance 
and operation of the licencee's serv ice shall be required to obtain 
security clearance from the Government of India prior to their 
deployment; 
• All content provided by the DTH platform to the subscribers, 
irrespective of its source, shall pass through the encryption and 
conditional access system, located within the earth station situated on 
Indian soil; 
• The licensee shall ensure that its facilities are not used for 
transmission of any objectionable or obscene content, messages or 
communication inconsistent with the laws of India; 
• The licensee shall provide the necessary facility for continuous 
monitoring of the DTH broadcasting service at its own cost and 
maintain the recordings of programmes and advertisements carried on 
the platform for a period of ninety days from the date of broadcast and 
produce the same to the licensor or its authorized representative, as and 
when required; 
• The licensee will, if required by the licensor or its authorized 
representative, provide necessary facilities for continuous monitoring 
for any particular aspect of the licensee's activities and operations; 
• the applicant is required to fulfil the eligibility criteria laid down in the 
DTH guidelines and is also subject to security and technical clearances 
from the concerned departments. 
The guidelines are available on this Ministry's website: mib.nic.in.

Entry of old vessels in ports 
108. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Paris MOU, an organisation of 20 IMO 
member countries, that monitors international standards has stipulated 
275 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
that certain categories of old vessels would be disallowed from entering its 
member ports without permission and inspection of its safety standards; 
(b) whether 36.5 per cent of our vessels which are 20 years old and 42.5 
per cent which are 10 years old would be affected; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING (SHRI 
DILIP KUMAR MANSUKHLAL GANDHI):(a) Yes Sir. Paris MOU, a 
regional organization of 20 IMO member countries mainly from the European 
Region established to co-ordinate Po rt State Control inspections in the 
Region, is going to introduce some new requirements with effect from 22nd 
July, 2003 on all the vessels entering ports of its member countries. Under the 
new requirements, some of the vessels may be refused access on the basis of 
number of detentions under Port State Control in the Paris MOU region in the 
previous 2 years. 
(b) and (c) There is no separate category proposed to be created under the 
new requirements between vessels of 10 years age and vessels of 20 years age 
and over. Categorization of the vessels under the new requirements which 
will be subjected to mandatory expanded inspection every 12 months is on the 
following lines : 
• Oil tankers over 3000 GRT and over 15 years old. 
• Chemical and Gas carriers over 10 years old. 
• Bulk carriers over 12 years old. 
• Passenger ships over 15 years old. 
In addition, new stipulation relates to inspection of ship on the basis of 
target factor which includes elements like previous inspection records of the 
ship, flag states rating based on performance of its ship under Paris MOU, 
classification status, type and age of the vessels. Any vessel, which has a 
target factor of 50 or more will be subjected to monthly inspections, if it calls 
Paris MOU member countries ports. Since the criteria as stated above are not 
based on age of the vessels being 
276 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
over 20 years and 10 years, the projected percentage figures are not apply. 
However, considering the Port State Control detention details of Indian ships 
since January 2002 under Paris MOU, no Indian ship comes in the above 
categories i.e. the ships which can be refused access or will be required to be 
inspected every month. In so far as expanded inspection requirements are 
concerned, Indian tankers, passenger sh ips, chemical and gas carriers do not 
generally operate in Paris MOU region . Therefore the new requirements of 
expanded inspections will affect only the Indian bulk carriers of over 12 years 
in age and most of Indian bulk carrier s are in this age group. However, under 
the Safety Convention requirements all the ships are required to be in full 
readiness always to undergo expanded inspections successfully.

Scavengers in the country 
110.    SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EM POWERMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of scavengers in the country as in 1992 and 2002, State-
wise; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Government have taken up a scheme called 
the National Scheme for Liberation and Rehabilitation of scavengers to 
liberate scavengers in 1992; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the number of people liberated so far under this scheme since 1992, 
State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JU STICE AND EMPOWERMENT (DR. 
SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): (a) A Statement-I is annexed. (See below). 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The National Scheme of Liberation and 
Rehabilitation of scavengers and their dependents (NSLRS) was launched in 
1991 -92 with the objective of providing financial assistance 
281 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
to scavengers for their training and rehabilitation in alternate occupations. Under 
the Scheme, assistance is provided for training in the institutes run by the 
State Governments', local bodies and NGOs as per TRYSEM norms. The 
training is given for a maximum duration of 6 months with a Stipend @ Rs. 
200 to Rs. 500 per month. 
Apart from assistance for training, the scavengers are assisted in 
taking up alternate occupation projects costing upto Rs. 50,000/- which 
is supported by a 50% subsidy, subject to a ceiling of Rs. 10,000.15% 
of the project cost, as a margin money loan provided to the beneficiary, 
is shared between the Central Government and State Governments in 
the ratio of 49:51.  
(d)The State-wise number of Scavengers assisted under the Scheme is given 
at Statement-ll.

.     125.      SHRI N.R. DASARI: 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of URB AN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  Municipalities in the small and 
medium towns are facing fiscal stress b ecause of their inability of increase 
upon their principal sources of revenue; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the remedial measures proposed to be taken 
by Government to improve the functioning of the municipalities in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) and (b) Municipalities, particularly in small and 
medium towns were facing fiscal difficulties due to their limited financial 
298 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
resources as well as limited access to generate revenue. A provision was, 
therefore made in the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 1992 itself for 
constitution of Finance Commissions at the State level in every five years to 
review the financial position of the municipalities and make recommendations 
to the State Government with regard to taxation; sharing of taxes between the 
State Government and Local Government; principles for governing grant-in-
aid; and measures for improving the financial position of urban local bodies. 
Suitable amendment has also been made to Article 280 of the Constitution to 
make it mandatory that the Central Finance Commission shall, inter-alia, 
make specific recommendations with regard to measures that are needed to 
augment the resources of a State with a view to supplementing the resources 
of municipalities in the State Fina nce Commission. This amendment has 
helped setting up of a proper linkage among local bodies, State Government 
and the Central Government. 
The State Governments have amended their Municipal Laws to devolve 
adequate functional and financial powers to municipalities in conformity 
with the provisions enshirned in the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act. 
However, as per Entry 5 of the State List of the Constitution, 
'municipality' is a State Subject. In view of this, it is for the State 
Governments to take necessary steps in augmenting financial resources of the 
municipalities and assisting them to come out of the fiscal stress, thereby 
improving their functioning. Nevertheless, the Government of India have 
initiated a number of schemes/programmes to bring in fresh breeze of reforms 
in the urban sector. These include: 
• Setting up of Urban Reforms Incentive Fund to provide reform-linked 
assistance to States with an initial allocation of Rs. 500 crores in the 
Union Budget 2002-03; 
• State-level Pooled Financing Structure to facilitate small and medium 
size urban local bodies to access capital market for investment in 
essential municipal infrastructure, development or bankable urban 
infrastructure projects and introduction of necessary reforms (e.g. tariff 
& financial) in the urban local bodies; 
• Tax-free Municipal Bonds for issue by urban local bodies for 
299 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
potable water supply, sewerage or sanitation, drainage, solid waste 
management, roads/bridges/flyovers, and urban transport. In addition, 
the Central Government has announced tax exemption in case of bonds 
issued by municipal/local Governments for raising resources for urban 
infrastructure. 
• Setting up of a City Challenge Fund for catalysing city level 
economic reform programmes. 
• Public-Private Participation Guidelines are prepared for providing 
directions to States and municipalities to manage the process of 
involving the private sector in infrastructure development. 
• The Minsitry issued Property Tax Guidelines in 1988 to all State 
Governments with the objective of simplification and rationalization 
of property tax, which is considered as one of the best source of 
revenue for the urban local bodies. States like Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, 
Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka are in the process of 
implementing property tax reforms.

drinking water demand for Hyderabad city as assessed by the Hyderabad 
Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board for the years 2004, 2016 and

{See below).

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION 
Withdrawal of Charges by CBI against highly placed accused 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Sir, what about the 
motion which we had given to you to raise a discussion under rule 170? 
Notice has been given under rule 168, and the discussion should take place 
under 170. I have pointed out in the motion that we would not like to interfere 
with the functioning of the Judiciary or any sub judice matter, but, surely, 
from the precedents which have been followed on earlier occasions, 
330 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
there is a scope that even if a motion appears, partly, to be sub judice, the part 
which is not sub judice can be discussed, and it has been discussed in the past. 
Once it was discussed in a motion moved by Shri N.G. Ranga on 7 th April, 
1966, and, again, in another motion on 16 th of November, 1971. It was 
discussed; though the motion appeared to be sub judice, the Speaker gave a 
ruling that if the entire matter was not sub judice, a part of it could be 
discussed. I have given a motion for discussion and I am reading that motion : 
"This House is of the opinion that the partisan manner in which CBI is 
utilized to abuse the legal process, to subvert the rule of law in the Babri 
Masjid Demolition case, is highly condem nable." This issue is agitating the 
mind of the people due to which we could not transact the normal business in 
the Question Hour today morning. A similar thing happened in the other 
House also, but I am not making any re ference to that. What we said on the 
floor of this House is that we re quire a satisfactor y response from the 
Government on various issues which have arisen in connection with the 
withdrawal of the charge -sheet where certain persons were accused of 
hatching a conspiracy under IPC 120 (B). It was not in the original FIR which 
was brought, but, subsequently, in the course of investigations, over a long 
period of time, another FIR was filed. Thereafter, the CBI submitted a 
consolidated FIR which was taken note of, taken cognisance of, by the Court. 
In course of time, certain legal infirmities came up. The higher Judiciary 
directed the Executive to rectify those, but nothing has happened. In between, 
just two weeks before, we were confronted with a situation that the status quo 
ante, prevailing in the first FIR almost ten years ago, has been restored. And 
whatever investigation has been done by the CBI in this case -- and the CBI 
was working under the direct control of  the Chief of the Union Executive, 
that is, the Prime Minister -- they ha ve simply withdrawn the cases against 
some of the very highly placed accused. To our assessment of the situation, 
this is not only a misuse of the CBI as an investigating agency, but is also 
subverting the rule of law by influencing the judicial process which is on. We 
have no intention to influence the decision of the court in either way. It is for 
the court to decide on the basis of the merits of the witnesses on the evidences 
which are being produced, but the investigating agency which is working 
directly under the Government of India, of which the Prime Minister is 
responsible, if they do certain things  which are not properly appreciated by 
the wider public opinion of this country, then, definitely, Parliament should 
have the right to discuss it and to arrive at its own conclusion. Keeping that 
objective in view, we have tabled this Motion.   And, most respectfully, Sir, I 
331 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
would like to submit to you to kindly allow this Motion to be debated. Let the 
House express its opinion. Let the legal aspects and political aspects be 
debated and discussed without having any interference with the due process 
of law, without having any reflection in  the course of trial which will take 
place independently in the respective c ourts. Parliament has nothing to do 
with it, but, surely, Parliament has ever y right to express its opinion when the 
premier investigating agency of the country is being misued or is being 
abused to subvert the due process of law. With these observations, Sir, I 
submit it for your consideration. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (W est Bengal): Sir, I will just briefly add 
to what Mr. Mukherjee ha s said as all of us, across the Opposition, have 
jointly signed the notice which we have served. Now, Sir, in the very 
beginning of the assumption of office by this Government, we had expressed 
our apprehension that we are going towards a situation where- so far as the 
Babri Masjid demolition case is concer ned-- the accused and the prosecution 
are one and the same. And, there was a clear-cut conflict of interest. 
Therefore, at any given point in time,  there may arise a situation where we 
will find that the prosecution has been sabotaged and the entire judicial 
process has been subverted and undermined, and it is precisely that is what 
has happened. The original investigation which was undertaken by the CID 
which was found inadequate, which was expanded. And, the CBI submitted 
the expanded chargesheet. Now, we see a particular provision of law being 
dropped from that chargesheet and the evidence that was collected by the CBI 
being dropped by the Government in the latest chargesheet which is being 
submitted. Therefore, Sir, in the fitness of things, it is our case that the 
conduct of the prosecution is very much  an issue in which the Executive is 
involved and Parliament is well within its right to discuss that issue and give 
its opinion. 
Sir, we will just give a parallel example. Last year, after the Godhra 
incident, when, in Gujarat, communal clashes and communal attacks took 
place against minorities, the National Human Rights Commission had given a 
suggestion that some of the major cases including the Godhra incident itself 
and four other major cases including the Best Bakery case should be tried by 
the CBI. I distinctly remember that the hon. Law Minister -- he is also here 
today - mentioned, "that will sabotage the prosecution because the 
investigation and prosecution by the ag encies there are at a very advanced 
stage, in all these cases. Therefore, if  we now go to CBI, that will sabotage 
and undermine the prosecution."     Now, we have

this country, and as representatives of the people, we are duty-bound to raise 
this issue. Sir, we have full faith in you that you will facilitate the process

Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 provides that 
the Central Government shall not enhance the rate of royalty in respect of 
any mineral more than once during any period of three years. The Act does

to revision of royalty rates on coal which inter-alia include that royalty rates 
on minerals be revised regularly and the decision about the revision of the 
rates of royalty be taken well before the date on which the revision falls due

Disaster mitigation programme in Orissa 
312.    SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR:

(a) whether it is a fact that Orissa State was in the grip of calamities 5 
times during the last five years and properties worth 150 billion were 
destroyed; 
(b) whether National Disaster Mitigation Committee has suggested 
implementation of special disaster mitigation programme in the State since it 
frequently gets hit by one or the other natural calamity; and 
(c) if so, the help rendered by the Centre to formulate a long-term plan to 
render assistance and control frequent lo ss of lives and property in such an 
eventuality? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SWAMI CHINMAYANAND): (a) Orissa was affected by super 
79 

RAJYA  SABHA [23 July, 2003] 
Cyclone in 1999, drought in 2000, flood in 2001 and drought in 2002. The 
total loss of property due to these disasters was substantial. It is not feasible to 
access the exact financial implications of the overall losses in community and 
private assets due to these calamities. 
(b)The Government of India has been stressing the need for greater 
emphasis on disaster prevention and mitigation programmes, besides relief and 
rehabilitation. The recommendations made to States including Orissa in this 
regard inter-alia focus on the establishment of State Disaster Management 
Authority, formation of specialized s earch and rescue teams, integratng 
disaster mitigation concerns with development plans, drawing up of disaster 
management plans at the State, district and village levels preparation of specific 
hazard related plans for hazard prone district maintenance of online inventory of 
resources for disaster management, training, education, awareness etc. The 
State Government has taken several steps for disaster preparedness and 
mitigation which inter-alia include setting up of Orissa State Disaster 
Mitigation Authority, development of sp ecialized search and rescue teams, 
implementation of community based disaster preparedness programmes in ten 
coastal blocks, construction of 102 multi-purpose cyclone shelters, 901 high 
school-cum-cyclone shelters, 549 primary schools which can be used as 
cyclone shelters, improvement of 215 health institutions, strengthening of district 
control rooms, procurement of relief line equipments, and awareness 
generation. 
(c) The Government of India has been extending advice and support to the 
State Governments including Orissa in the formulation of long term disaster 
management plans; and building up capacity. The Central Government has 
also released an assistance of Rs. 999. 47 crore to Government of Orissa from 
the National Calamity Contingency Fund during 1999-2000 to 2002-2003, 
besides Centre's share of assistance under the Calamity Relief Fund.

Subject: Optimisation of direct recruitment to civilian posts. 
The Finance Minister while presenting the Budget for 2001-2002 has 
stated that "all requirements of.recruitment will be scrutinised to ensure that 
fresh recruitment is limited to 1 per cent of total civilian staff strength. As 
about 3 per cent of staff retire every y ear, this will reduce the manpower by 2 
per cent per annum achieving a reduction of 10 per cent in five years as 
announced by the Prime Minister". 
1.2 The Expenditure Reforms Commission had also considered the issue 
and had recommended that each Minist ry/Department may formulate annual 
Direct Recruitment Plans through the mechanism of Screening Committees. 
2.1 All Ministries/Departments are accordingly requested to prepare Annual 
Direct Recruitment Plans covering the requirements of all cadres, whether 
managed by that Ministry/Department itself, or managed by the Department 
of Personnel & Training etc. The task of preparing the Annual Recruitment 
Plan will be undertaken in each Ministry/Department by a Screening Committee 
headed by the Secretary of that Mini stry/ Department with the Financial 
Adviser as a Member and JS (Admn.) of the Department as Member Secretary. 
The Committee would also have one senior representative each of the Department 
of Personnel & Training and the Department of Expenditure. While the annual 
Recruitment Plans for vacancies in Groups 'B', 'C and 'D' could be cleared by this 
Committee itself, in the case of Group 'A' Services, the Annual Recruitment 
Plan would be clreared by a Committe e headed by Cabinet Secretary with 
Secretary of the Department concerned, Secretary (DOPT) and Secretary 
(Expenditure) as Members. 
123 

RAJYA  SABHA [23 July, 2003] 
2.2 While preparing the annual Recruitment Plans, the concerned 
Screening Committees would ensure that direct recruitment does not in any 
case exceed 1 % of the total sanctioned strength of the Department. Since about 
3% of staff retire every year, this would translate into only 1/3rd of the direct 
recruitment vacancies occurring in each year being filled up. Accordingly, 
direct recruitment would be limited to 1/3rd of the direct recrutiment vacancies 
arising in the year subject to a further ceiling that this does not exceed 1% of the 
total sanctioned strength of the Department. While examing the vacancies to 
be filled up, the functional needs of the organisation would be critically 
examined so that there is flexibility in  filling up vacancies in various cadres 
depending upon their relative functional need. To amplify, in case an organisation 
needs certain posts to be filled up for safety/security/operational 
considerations, a corresponding reducti on in direct recruitment in other 
cadres of the organisation may be done with a view to restricting the overall 
direct recruitment to one-third of vacancies meant for direct recruitment subject 
to the condition that the total vacancies proposed for filling up should be within 
the 1% ceiling.' The remaining vacancies meant for direct recruitment which 
are not cleard by the Screening Committees will not be filled up by promotion 
or otherwise and these posts will stand abolished. 
2.3 While the Annual Recruitment Plan would have to be prepared 
immediately for vacancies anticipated in  2001 -02, the issue of filling up of 
direct recruitment vacancies existing on  the date of issue of these orders, 
which are less than one year old and for which recruitment action has not yet

362. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of 
PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the pay and perks of Government officials in 
India is far below their counterparts in the established private organizations; 
125 
 

RAJYA  SABHA [23 July, 2003] 
(b) whether any study has been conducted to assess the pay and perks of 
Government officials vis-a-vis those in the comparable posts in private sector; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) if not, whether Government propose to undertake such a study to 
rationalize and arrive at the realistic level of pay and perks for Government 
employees in sync with prevailing international trend and practices, and 
(e) if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) to 
(c) So far as the issue of comparison of pay and perks of Government officials 
with their counterparts in the private s ector is concerned, the same cannot be 
compared as the pay and perks in the pr ivate sector are invariably detrmined 
by the market forces which is not so in the case of Government employees. It 
may, therefor, not be correct to hold that the pay and perks of Government 
officials in India is far below their counterparts in the established private 
organizations. The exercise of pay revi son and pay determination for Central 
Government employees is performed by Pay Commission, constituted for this 
purpose, by the Central Government. The last pay revision for Central 
Government employees was carried out based on recommendations of the 
Fifth Central Pay Commission. The Pay Commissions are expert bodies which 
take a holistic view on revision of pay scales, based on the various inputs, 
including a study of pay scales in privat e sector. Various facilities and perks 
including high job security, post-retirement benefits etc., available to Central 
Government employees are also taken into consideration while 
recommending revision of pay scales and allowances. Views of Fifth Central 
Pay Commisison is this regard are available in their report, which is a 
published document.

(e) Does not arise.

Reduction in power thefts 
376. SHRI G.K. VASAN: Will the Mini ster of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether there has been a reduction in power theft in 2002-2003; 
(b) if so, the State-wise details of such reduction; and 
(c) if not, the steps proposed to be taken to reduce power theft? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATIJAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) As per Central Elctricity Authority; 
the figures for reduction in power theft in 2002-03 are not available. 
(b) Does not arise in view of reply to (a) above. 
(c) The Elctricity Act, 2003 provides a legal framework for making theft 
of electricity a cognizable offence. U nder Section 135 of the electricity Act, 
2003, whoever dishonestly taps lines or  cables or service wires, tampers 
damages or destroys meters etc., shall be punishable with imprisonment for a 
term which may extend to three years or with fine or with both. A scheme is 
being implemented to grant incentives for State Governments/Power Utilities 
which show reduction in cash losses, a significant portion of which is because 
of theft of power.

Reforms Programme (APDRP) which is intended for Upgradation of 
Sub-Transmission and Distribution in densely electrified zones in the 
urban and industrial areas and improvement in commercial viability 
of State Electricity Boards by re ducing the aggregate technical and 
commercial (AT & C) losses to around 15% as against the existing 
over 50%. During the year 2002-03 the Government has sanctioned

Private participation in power sector 
378. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a)  whether it is a fact that desp ite the aggressive reforms and 
encouragement by the Gove rnments, the growth of private sector in power 
sector is very slow; 
(b)  if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c)  the State-wise details of the capac ity addition by private sector since 
1991. 
(d)  whether it is also a fact that privat e sector could not realize its target 
in Ninth Plan and in the first year of Tenth Plan; 
(e)  the reasons for the slippage of the target; and 
(f)  the steps being taken by Union and State Governments to clear the 
road blocks for greater private participation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The main reasons for slow growth of private sector in power sector 
are indicated below:- 
(i)  Failure to achieve financial closure inspite of good progress on other 
fronts due to insistence by the financial institutions on State 
149

financial condition of the State Electricity Boards/Transmission 
companies. 
(ii)  Delay in finalization of various  contracts such as Power Purchase 
Agreement, Implementation Agreement, Fuel Supply Agreement and 
Fuel Transportation Agreement, etc. 
(iii)  Court cases/litigation in the form of public interest petition, etc. 
(iv)   Increase in the prices of liquid fuels such as naphtha. 
(v) With drawal by equity holders and EPC (Engineering, Procurement & 
Construction) contractors. 
The situation is expected to improve once the State owned utilities turn 
around and become financially sound.

(f) In addition to assisting the State Governments in the reform and 
restructuring of their power sect or and providing assistance under 
programmes like the Accelerated Po wer Development Reforms Programme 
(APDRP), financing of power projects based on reforms linked mile stones has 
been envisaged. The Government is also providing funds to private sector through

403. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether government are awar e that powerloom owners in 
Maharashtra are facing problems and seeking Central Government's 
help;

what effective steps have been taken for the benefit of powerloom sector in 
Maharashtra; and 
(c) if so the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANAGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) to (c) The major problems facing the 
decentralised powerloom units of the country including those in Maharashtra 
include:— 
  (i)  Technological obsolescence 
 (ii)  Small size of units with fragmentation 
(iii) High power tariffs with uncertain power supply 
(iv)  Lack of credit availability 
(v)  Poor marketability 
(vi)  Low skill level and poor quality consciousness. 
2. Government has taken several initiatives to mitigate their hardships 
and facilitate growth of the decentralized powerloom industry, including those 
in Maharashtra, to become competitive and face the global challenge. These

Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) whereby the powerloom 
owner can reduce the cost of borrowi ng capital either by availing 12% 
upfront Capital Linked Subsidy or by obtaining 5% interest 
reimbursement of the loan availed. 
(ii) Import duty on shuttleless looms has been reduced and excise duty 
exemption has been given to indigenous automatic looms. Accelerated 
depreciation benefits at the rate of 50% have been extended on the 
weaving machinery installed under TUFS.

shuttleless looms has been brought from 15% to 5%.

courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in the field of design, merchandising and 
marketing.

Need to check T.B. menace in tribal tracts of Orissa 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Madam, my Special Mention relates to the 
threat of tuberculosis to tribal people, particularly in Orissa, and elsewhere 
also. Some say that "Every minute one person dies of tuberculosis in India and 
every second one gets infected with TB." This may or may not be true. But, 
recent studies show that in Orissa alone, 18,000 people die on an average 
annually, particularly in the tribal tracts  of the State. About one lakh women 
are driven out of their homes on suspicio n of being TB-patients. If parents are 
afflicted, their children are denied admi ssion to schools or are expelled from 
the classes. While extreme poverty, substandard food, unhealthy homes and 
surroundings are some of the causes for spread of TB, lack of awareness 
among the people subscribes to the growing social stigma to add to the misery 
of the afflicted families. Added to such tragedies, medical personnel in tribal 
tracts are not well-trained to treat the patients. It was detected in" a conference 
of doctors held at Sunabeda in the trib al tracts, in the year 2002 that 75 per 
cent of the doctors prescribed wrong medicines for TB-cure. Worse than this is 
that serious steps are not taken to detect the disease among the children who 
are left to the mercy of quacks by ignorant rural poor. Such patients do not 
respond to proper treatment when diseas e- develops because of the effect of 
wrong medicines used earlier. Since TB-affected wage-earners migrate to 
different areas for work, TB also spreads to other human settlements, 
particularly to urban slums. I appeal to the hon. Minister of Health and to the 
Government of India to take appropriate measures to prevent growing 
incidence of Tuberculosis in wide tracts of tribal Orissa. The State Government 
may also be alerted.

second visit to Bangladesh in the last twelve months, in Bangladesh on the 14th and

ten years is imported into Nepal every month and it is being dumped into

Member has asked. In negotiating free trad e agreements, we take care to have 
a provision about "value added" and this is negotiated as to how much value 
should be added, whether it should be 50 per cent or whether it should be 60

the problem that if that country with which we have an agreement is importing

qualify for duty free treatment. This is one point, Sir. The other is, you look at 
our tariffs. Our tariffs are also coming down. In case the tariff regime itself is 
harmonised to an extent, that takes care of cheaper import of raw materials 
and even finished goods. At the same time, I must also say that what we are 
trying to create in South Asia is a win-win situation for all the countries in 
this region. India, as the largest country, must play its role very responsibly, 
as a promoter of this concept of cooperation between the SAARC countries in 
the region. This is the broader vision that we have and this must always be kept 
in mind. So far as the question on vanaspati and other things is concerned, we 
have even been permitted by the WTO the concept of tariff quota where we

entered into in 1972, reiterated in 1973, reiterated in 1980, reiterated in 1997 
and 1999 where they have agreed to give us transit and transhipment rights.

mainly through the inland water route. So  far as railway and road transits are 
concerned, Bangladesh's point has been that it is not fit enough or strong 
enough or adequate enough to be able to take the load of the transit of goods 
which will move from one part of India to another. This is something that we 
are continually discussing with them. The reply to the question is the two are 
not contingent on each other.

*63. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Prime Minister attende d the G-8 Summit at France held 
on June 1, 2003; 
(b) if so, the subject discussed there at and decisions arrived; 
(c) whether the Prime Minister advocated phasing out of trade-distorting 
movement of personnel for providing services, elimination of tariff and non-
tariff barriers to exports of developing countries and monitoring and 
evaluating the outcomes of the Doha round of WTO negotiations; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of the summit on these issues? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI YASHWANT 
SINHA): (a) to (d) A statement is attached. 
Statement 
Prime Minister participated in the G-8 Enlarged Dialogue in Evian on 1st 
June 2003 at the invitation of Presiden t Chirac. There wa s a free and frank 
exchange of views on development assistance to developing countries, transfer 
of technologies, environment related issues and trade barriers that affect 
developing countries. The Enlarged Dialogue was the first of its kind and was 
not intended to produce a formal Summit document. Its intention was to 
articulate concerns of developing countries and exchange views with developed 
countries on the above issues. 
PM expressed disappointment at the lack of progress so far on the 
Millennium Development Round since the Doha meeting. PM underlined the 
need to eliminate tariff and non-tariff barriers, especially phasing out all trade 
distorting agricultural subsidies, removal of restrictions on the free movement 
of natural persons for providing serv ices and broader access of developing 
countries to pharmaceuticals. 
The issues raised by PM were also re flected in the statements of some of 
the other developing country participants in the Enlarged Dialogue. While 
there was no formal comment by the G8 on the issues

some of the concerns of developing countries. It reiterated the importance of 
improved market access for all WTO members, especially for developing

expressed commitment for their general development.

High technology cooperation with U.S. 
*67. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Prime Minister during his visit to New York 
in last September referred to the scope in high technology co-operation; and 
(b) if so, the details if fields where such co-operation has started? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) and (d) During their meeting in 
New York on 12 September 2002, Prime Minister and U.S. President George 
W. Bush agreed to explore possibilities of expanding cooperation in space, 
diverse forms of energy, high-technology commerce and science. 
India and the United States have initiated five safety related projects for 
safeguarded nuclear facilities. Exchange of visits by U.S. and Indian nuclear 
regulatory officials has also commenced . In the area of space, the two sides 
have renewed the Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in earth 
and atmospheric sciences. The United States has offered to resume co-
operation in space, appli cations for sustainable development, whether 
research missions, tele-medicine, tele-education and disaster management. 
Joint workshops on civilian space application and research have also started. 
The two sides have established a bilateral High Technology Cooperation 
Group, which held its first meeting in Washington D.C. on 1 -2 July 2003. 
This is the first such group that the United States has set up with any country. 
The Group discussed regulatory and promotional issues related to enhancing 
trade in 'dual use' goods and technologies, as well as facilitating cooperation 
in areas such as information technolo gy, life sciences, nano-technology and 
defence technology. 
The two sides are also pursuing co llaborative science and technology 
projects in the areas of health and communicable diseases, environment and 
climate change, and renewable and clean energy. Under the aegis of the 1998 
agreement between Department of Science and Technology and the U.S. 
National Science Foundation, there are currently about 65   scientific 
research projects supported by various labs, 
29 

RAJYA  SABHA [24 July, 2003] 
institutions and universities in India and U.S.A. The India-U.S. Science and 
Technology Forum was established in 2000 to catalyse India-U.S. scientific 
collaboration.

524. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state": 
(a) whether the Second Labour Commission's recommendations to 
"rationalise" labour laws for liberalisation are being processed and any time-
frame has been evolved to conclude this exercise;

Conference and several seminars held during the last year, have been 
consolidated; and

Commission's recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) The Second National Commission on Labour 
(NCL) in its report submitted to the Government on 29.06.2003 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2003] 
had made wide-ranging recommendati ons on various facets of labour viz. 
review of laws, social security, women & child labour, skill development, wages, 
labour administration, unorganised sector, etc. The recommendations have 
been receiving utmost attention of the Government. The Ministry has already 
held detailed consultations and interactions with the workers representatives, 
employers organisations, experts & professionals etc. The Report of the 
Commission was discussed at the 38th Session of Indian Labour Conference 
held on 28-29 September, 2002, a National Seminar on Unorganised Sector

participative management and consolidation of social security legislation and 
establishment of social security sytstem.

Labour Laws 
532. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Second Labour Commission's recommendations to 
rationalise labour laws for liberalisation has not made any progress for 
the last one year; 
(b) whether the labour reforms with amendment to Industrial Disputes 
Act and the Contract Labour Act rate are also pending; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps being taken to get them expedited? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) to (d) The Second National Commission on 
Labour (NCL) in its report submitted to  the Government on 29.06.2003 has 
made wide-ranging recommendations on various facets of labour viz. review 
of laws, social security, women & child labour, skill development, wages, 
labour administration, unorganised sector, etc. The recommendations have 
been receiving utmost attention of the Government. The Ministry has already 
held intensive consultations and interactions with the workers representatives, 
employers organisations, experts & professionals etc. The Report of the 
Commission was discussed at the 38th Session of Indian Labour Conference 
held on 28-29September, 2002, a National Seminar on Unorganised Sector 
Workers on 7-8 November 2002 and a Tripartite Committee Meeting held on 
18-19 February 2003. The report was also discussed at the Consultative 
Committee meeting held on 30.04.2003. Based on these deliberations, a Bill 
on Umbrella Legislation for Workers in the Unorganised Sector is likely to be 
introduced in the current session of the Parliament. The amendment proposals 
in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and Contract Labour (Regulation and 
Abolition) Act, 1970 have been under consideration of the Government for 
some time. At the moment, further changes in the amendment proposal of 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947  is being contemplated in the light of NCL's 
recommendations. The matter relating to amendment proposals in respect of 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolitio n) Act, 1970 is under consderation 
of the Group of Ministers and is yet to be finalised.

SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL: Madam, I have great pleasure in 
introducing this Motion. The purpose of introducing this Motion is to review 
ten years of implementation of the Part IX and IX-A of the Constitution 
dealing with Panchayats and Municipalities as institutions of self-
government. The Constitution (73 rd Amendment) Act, 1992 dealing with 
Panchayats, which came into force with effect from 24 th April, 1993 is a 
landmark in the history of Panchayats.   With this amendment a three-tier 
structure of governance 
203 

 
RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2003] 
was introduced in the rural areas of our federal polity. Elections were made 
compulsory every five years to the th ree tiers. Reservations were introduced 
for SCs/STs and Women and a separate domain of 29 subjects was listed out 
for the Panchayats to function. 
Today, ten years after the passing of the 73rd Amendment Act, after a 
lot of efforts, we have been able to achieve regular conduct of elections, give 
effect to reservation of seats for Sc heduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and 
Women, appoint State Finance Commissions and State Election 
Commissions. Panchayat elections have been heid in all the States, except 
Jharkhand and the Union Territory of Pondicherry. We have around 2.50 lakh 
Panchayats of which about 2.25 lakh are Gram Panchayats. Approximately 30 
lakh persons have been elected to these Panchayats of whom more than 10 
lakh are women giving us the largest representative base anywhere in the 
world. While appreciating the efforts so far made by our State Governments in 
enacting the required legislations in their respective States to implement the 
provisions of the 73rd Amendment Act, 1993, I have to stress that still a lot of 
ground has to be covered to strengthen Panchayati Raj Institutions. Much 
remains to be done in the field of devolution of financial and administrative 
powers to Panchayats. While some States have devolved powers on 
Panchayats, many others are yet to make a beginning. States which devolved 
powers vary in the extent and type of devolution. While some States have 
devolved more powers upon District and Intermediate Panchayats, some 
others have devolved powers only on the Gram Panchayats and Intermediate 
Panchayats, ignoring the District Panchayats. Most States, after devolving 
several responsibilities on the PRIs, have not transferred the requisite staff and 
funds in respect of the subjects transf erred to Panchayats, which are essential 
to carrying out the responsibilities entrusted on them. Besides, Panchayats 
must be given commensurate powers to levy and collect their own taxes, and 
generate their own resources. Only wh en resources are made available and 
administrative powers given to Panchayats, would they be able to take care of 
local level needs and function as institutions of self government. 
States are also found to be wanting in constituting District Planning 
Committees, holding regular Gram Sabha meetings and building in 
accountability of Panchayats. There is also a need for revamping and aligning 
the election machinery, the audit mach inery and the Finance Commissions in 
the States to bring them in line with their counterpart institutions at the 
Centre. 
204 

(24 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
To enable the institution of Panchayats to function in an effective 
manner, the Gram Sabhas have to be vested with responsibilities such as 
supervision and monitoring the functioning of the Gram Panchayats, approval 
of plans and selection of beneficiaries and projects, mobilization of 
contribution in cash or kind such as voluntary labour for community welfare 
projects and promotion of unity and harmony among all sections of society. 
Gram Sabhas have yet to be empowered in an effective manner in most 
States.

There are many among us who have come from the Tribal regions. 
The provisions of Panchayats (Extension to the Schedule V Areas) Act, 1996 
extends the provisions of the 73 rd Amendment Act to Schedule V Areas to 
give the benefit of local self-government to predominantly tribal areas. The 
PESA Act provides, that every legislation on the Panchayats in Schedule V 
Areas should be in conformity with the customary laws, social and religious 
practices and traditional management of community resources. It provides for 
100 per cent reservation for Scheduled Tribes for the seat of Chairpersons at 
all levels of the Panchayats and proportionate but not less than 50 per cent of 
the total number of seats of Members to be reserved for Scheduled Tribes in 
all tiers of Panchayats. The Act vests wide ranging powers in the Gram 
Sabhas in Scheduled Areas such as mandatory consultations with Gram 
Sabha prior to land acquisition, entrustment of planning and management of 
water bodies to Gram Sabha, mandatory requirement of Gram Sabha 
recommendations for grant of prospec ting licence or mining lease or for 
exploration of minor minerals. The Act also vests in the Gram Sabha the 
power to enforce prohibition to restrict the sale and consumption of 
intoxicants. It vests in the Gram Sabha the ownership of minor forest 
produce, powers to manage village markets; to exercise control over money-
lending to the Scheduled Tribes; and control local plans and resources 
including tribal sub plans. The PESA Act extends to Tribal Areas of nine

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE : Thank you, Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, for permitting me to make some observations on the motion 
moved by the hon. Minister. A period of ten years, after the passage of the 
Seventy-third and Seventy-fourth Amendments to the Constitution, is, no 
doubt, a milestone in the process of consolidating the democratic structure of 
this country. Naturally, on this occasion our mind goes to that young man, 
who not only dreamt of the 21 st century but also visua lised that, to play an 
effective role in the 21 s1 century, there was a need to re-organise institutional 
structures and, primarily, to strengthen our basic democratic structure. Surely, 
I do feel that this House would be failing in its duty, if we do not gratefully 
remember the contributions made by late Rajiv Gandhi in strengthening the 
democratic structure of this country. After the Constitution was adopted in the 
early '50s, exactly speaking, on 26 th January, 1950--the work of drafting the 
Constitution was completed in November, 1949-there has been a sea-change. 
The type of democratic structure, whic h was contemplated at that point of 
time, was to have one Central Government and several Provincial" 
Governments. Of course, in the early years of our Reoublic we had different 
categories of States, ranging from Part-A  State to Part-D State. Nonetheless, 
the basic concept of our federation was that the Federal Government and the 
constituent units would enjoy power from the Constitution itself to play their 
role in the service of the nation. Toda y, when we are celebrating the tenth 
y6ar of Seventy-third and Seventy-f ourth Amendments to the Constitution, 
our population has increased by three times.    There are tremendous 
technological changes.

The Indian Constitution was framed in the backdrop of the Second World 
War. But when we passed the Seventy-third and Seventy-fourth Amendments 
a decade ago, for the first time, in the history of the world, we witnessed a 
long five decade, though there was the stress and strain of the Cold War, 
without having any major world war or international conflagration involving 
the nations, as we witnessed in the first half of the last century encompassing 
two world wars, that is, the First World War from 1914-1918 and the Second 
World War from 1939-1945. The world derived benefits from them, 
especially, in the areas of technology. In that context, it was absolutely 
necessary to strengthen the democratic structure of this country, not merely 
depending on 788 Members of Parliament, belonging to both Houses, and 
roughly about four thousand and a few hundred Members of the State 
Legislative Assemblies in different Stat es and a couple of hundred Members 
of the Legislative Councils. Today more than three million people, who are

SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU (Pondicherry): Thank you, Sir, 
for having given me this opportunity to speak on this Motion. I welcome the 
Motion. The 73 rd Amendment in the Constitution generated enthusiasm 
among the people. They thought that th ere will be a larger  participation of 
rural people, there will be democracy at  the grassroot level and there will be 
decentralisation of power throughout  India and the people would rule 
themselves. This was the slogan which was envisaged after the 73 rd 
Amendment. Even though the amendment has been made, the reality is that 
the Panchayats are toothless. 
Sir, I would like to read from a recent survey of Panchayats working 
in 19 States, conducted by the National Institute of Rural Development. It 
states as under: 
1) Absence of a national consensus across party lines on what 
should be the status of the PRIs. There has been no political 
initiative to empower the Gram Sabha (village council 
consisting of all voters) and to get the PRIs back on track 
for speedy rural development. 
2) High-level political authorities are unwilling to give up 
control over finance and development schemes. 
252 

[24 July, 
2003] 
RAJYA 
SABHA 
3) The stronghold of the bureaucracy over PRIs continues. 
4) Functional and financial autonomy has not been granted to 
the PRIs. 
5) PRIs are perceived as lower-level agencies of the 
government, diluting their conceived status as units of self-
government. 
6) There is a tendency to execute only schemes sponsored by 
the State or Union Government. Hardly any programmes 
are carried out from PRIs own resources. 
7) Most States have failed to give the Gram Sabha a mandate 
by clearly defining its functions and authority. This renders 
the Gram Sabha ineffective. 
8) There has been no transfer of general or technical staff by 
the State Governments to the PRIs. 
So, Sir, these are the eight defects which have been pointed out, and 
it is said that the Panchayats are toothless. Taking these facts into 
consideration. I believe the Government of India would like to make an 
amendment to the Constitution for strengthening the Panchayat system, as it 
is. 
Sir, I would further like to say that several district planning 
commissions have to be constituted as per the provisions of article 243(d) of 
the Constitution. It has already been said by Mr. Reddy that the DPCs are 
entrusted with the job of preparing composite plan, but it has to be headed by 
the elected bodies. What has happened is this. In certain States, Ministers 
have been appointed; in certain St ates, bureaucrats alone have been 
appointed; in certain States committees have not even been constituted. So, 
this is the tendency which is prevailing. 
Another thing I would like to say is, even when the Gram Panchayat 
is already constituted, the State Governments are interfering with their affairs 
by appointing parallel committees. The parallel committees are like water-
sharing committees, vigilance committees, village prohibition committees 
and village education committees. Thes e committees are, more or less, 
functioning as parallel Village Panchayat Committees, causing a lot of 
hindrance. The Prime Minister has also cautioned certain States saying 
253 

RAJYA SABHA      [24 July, 2003] 
not to constitute parallel committees which cause hindrance to the working of 
Panchayats. 
I have another worry and I would like to submit that before the 
august House. The Government of India has the Ministry of Rural 
Development. This Ministry is pumping crores of rupees to the Village 
Panchayats. This too is, more or less, working parallel to the Panchayats. The 
Ministry of Rural Development is pumping money like anything into the 
villages and this Ministry is functioning, more or less, parallel to the Village 
Panchayats. Instead of doing that, you assign all the functions to the Village 
Panchayats; let them do it as they want. Above all, the Rural Development 
Ministry has constituted District Vigilance and Monitoring Committees 
appointing Members of Parliament as the Chairmen of those committees. My 
worry is, on the one hand, we say not to constitute any committees that 
interfere with the working of Village Panchayats. On the other hand, we 
constitute committees like this and this, more or less, interferes with the 
working of the Village Panchayats. I request the hon. Minister to consider this 
aspect. You must ask the State Governme nts also not to encroach upon the 
working of Village Panchayats. I also request the Central Government not to 
interfere with the working of the Village Panchayats. 
I have another submission. In certain States, we are not able to 
conduct elections that are reserved for Scheduled Castes. What is the reason? 
In Tamil Nadu and several other places, elections are not conducted in places 
reserved for SCs because the SC peopl e are landless poor agriculturists, 
depending upon the caste Hindus. They also fear economic boycott. They fear 
that the economic boycott may be enforced against the dalit people, and that is 
why they are afraid of contesting electio ns. Moreover, they are landless, poor 
agricultural people and they don't want to have any quarrel with the rich 
agriculturists. On those grounds, they  are not able to contest elections. I 
request the Government to provide adequate security for those who want to 
contest elections. There should be a strong action against those who prevent 
dalits from contesting elections. Even after they get elected, they have been 
prevented from continuing in office, they resigned and went away. The civil 
society also should come forward to help those people. 
I would like also to say that we are making several amendments. 
Evert the Supreme Court has recently delivered a judgment in regard to 
254 

[24 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Members of Parliament and Legislativ e Assemblies, laying down what are 
the things the applicants should d eclare, at the time of filing their 
nominations. They have to declare their assets, their convictions and 
educational qualification. This also should be stipulated for those who want 
to contest Panchayat elections. It shou ld be incorporated in respect of 
Panchayat elections also. A person who wants to contest elections should 
declare all these facts before becoming a member of any body. I request the 
Minister to kindly take this into consideration. 
There is another thing to be considered. If a ruling party is in power 
in a particular State, and if the Opposition's party has won the election for 
Mayor's post, or, Chairman of any Village Panchayat or municipality, we are 
having a lot of difficulties. They are not getting financial assistance. Everyday, 
they are being humiliated. Everyday, they are being charged, and they are 
facing problems in the day-to-day functioning. A sort of pandemonium has 
been created. It should not be allowed to continue as it is now. In order to 
avoid this anomaly, there should be some law. If the elected bodies are 
headed by opposition parties, they also should be allowed to function without 
fear, and all kinds of facilities should be provided to them by the ruling party. 
If an agitation goes on in a State, now the Central Government says, "No, it is 
the State Government's job, we can't interfere." The same thing should be 
applied for the Panchayats also by the State Governments, even if they are 
ruled by opposition parties. The State Government should say, "We are not 
going to interfere with it, since it is a subject of the concerned municipalities 
and corporations." 
With these words, I support the motion. Thank you.

SHRI R.S. GAVAI (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, at the 
outset, I welcome the Motion moved by the hon. Minister, Mr. Patil, to 
consider the progress of the Panchayats and Municipalities as institutions of 
self-government during the last ten years. 
It does mean also that, while discussing about the progress of the Panchayat 
Raj, an inherently impression is that he is inviting some suggestions from us 
for the better implementation of the Act. Sir, coming to the Constitution 
(Seventy-third) Amendment Act, 1992, I would say that I will cover only four 
aspects. As an example, I deal with the progress of it and thereafter give some 
suggestions. The first aspect is Gram Sabha. The second aspect is District 
Planning and Development Committee. The third aspect is Extension to the 
Scheduled Area. The fourth and the last aspect is the subject given in the 
Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution. Sir, what is the purpose of the 
Constitution (Seventy-third) Amendment Act? It gives a constitutional status 
to Gram Sabha. Gram Sabha means a bo dy consisting of persons, registered 
in the electoral rolls, relating to a village comprised within the area of 
panchayat at the village level, Gram  Sabha may exercise such power and 
perform such functions at the village level as the Legislature of a State may, 
by law, provide. That is how villager, above the age of eighteen years, has an 
inherent right to determine his own destiny. Gram Sabha is the forum where 
the marginalized poor can influence th e decisions affecting their life. I do 
refer, of course, to the very purpose given in the Constitution, I would give 
the gist.    The role of the

Panchayat Raj institution at the village level. The role of the local people in 
conducting social audit and fixing the responsibility of the Panchayat

At the outset, I welcome it. The hon. Mi nister is from Maharashtra. I am also 
from Maharashtra. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether any 
Gram Panchayat has a Gram Sabha in Ma harashtra; whether all the citizens,

the Gram Sabha meetings, are invited there. The pious intention behind all 
this is being spoiled because of faulty implementation. Sir, it is my habit that 
whenever I go to a public function, I go to the Gram Panchayat or to the 
Sarpanch concerned and ask them to show me the register which has to be 
maintained by them to record the number of people, living below poverty line.

Gram Sabha, which never take place, are noted down in the register. This is

to find out who is at the helm of affairs, not to allow the people of villages to 
participate in the meetings of the Gram Sabha. Secondly, the criterion of 
'below poverty line' is the basis for the prospective progress of the people, 
who live below the poverty line. We know that thousands of crores of rupees 
are allotted by the Government of India, under the DRDA, at the district level 
for the very ambitious schemes to alleviate poverty. Indira Awas Yojna, 
Assurance Scheme, Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojna, Pradhan Mantri 
Svayam Rozgar Yojna are all very am bitious schemes. But what is the 
criterion for these schemes? The criteri on is that the individual beneficiary 
must be in the list of the people living below the poverty line. Secondly, what
